Notes from Chapter 3, **Databases and Data APIs**, of
[DevOps for Data Science](https://do4ds.com/chapters/sec1/1-3-data-access.html).
The working implementation lives in
[penguin-explorer](https://github.com/mpfoley73/penguin-explorer).
See also [Model Artifacts and Prediction APIs](model-artifacts-and-apis.qmd).
Examples below are reference snippets, not executable Quarto chunks.

## Why separate the layers?

A shared database gives R and Python the same stored source. A saved model
separates training from serving. An API lets an interface request predictions
without loading the model itself. Each piece has a clear responsibility and
can change independently, provided its interfaces remain compatible.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    D[(DuckDB: penguins)] --> E[R EDA report]
    D --> M[Python model training]
    M --> P[Saved model on Pins board]
    P --> A[Vetiver API: port 8080]
    U[Shiny interface: port 8000] -->|POST JSON inputs| A
    A -->|JSON prediction| U
```

The arrows show data and artifact flow, not one continuous request. Training
reads DuckDB and saves a model. The API loads that artifact; each button click
uses the loaded model without rerunning training or querying DuckDB.

## One database, two language clients

R and Python require their own DuckDB packages, installed in their respective
project environments (`renv` and `.venv`). Both clients can read the same
`my-db.duckdb` file. Use a consistent working directory so a relative filename
resolves to the intended database. Close connections when finished; a shared
file does not imply unrestricted concurrent writes from different processes.

Loading query results into an R data frame or pandas DataFrame brings the data
into memory. This differs from leaving a query lazy and computing in the
database. Our small example uses in-memory results.

Keep the original data intact, then filter for the model's required columns.
For example, `model_df = df.dropna(subset=model_columns)` excludes missing model
inputs without discarding rows for unrelated missing fields. Compute excluded
counts against the original `df`. In this project, 344 rows became 333 model
rows, with 11 excluded.

## A request is an explicit contract

The client sends a POST request to `http://127.0.0.1:8080/predict` with a JSON
list of observations:

```json
[
  {
    "bill_length_mm": 39.1,
    "species_Chinstrap": false,
    "species_Gentoo": false,
    "sex_male": true
  }
]
```

Both species indicators are false for Adelie, the reference category; the sex
indicator is true for Male. The field names and encoding must match the model's
saved input prototype. Python dictionaries use `True` and `False`; the requests
package serializes them to JSON's lowercase Boolean values.

The tested response had HTTP status 200 and this body:

```json
{"predict": [3988.8289177706565]}
```

That is a model estimate of about 3,989 grams, not an observed weight. Check HTTP
success before extracting the response: `response.raise_for_status()` surfaces
HTTP errors, and `response.json()["predict"][0]` extracts the first prediction.

## What I learned

The Shiny interface gathers inputs and displays output. The API owns prediction;
it loads the saved model. Both servers must be running, on different ports.
Changing a dropdown does not send a prediction request until the button is
clicked because `@reactive.event(input.predict)` gates the rendered calculation.

This separation is useful when multiple clients need the same prediction
service or when presentation changes independently of model training. It also
adds a process and an HTTP boundary to operate; a small app does not always
need a separate API.

Project-specific startup commands belong in the Penguin README. Dependency
records belong with their environments: `renv.lock` for R and
`requirements.txt` for Python. Neither record alone recreates the database or
saved model; those require the preparation and training steps too.
